title: XML formatter: CDATA, namespaces and entities
description: Site XML formatter and minifier: a fixed UTF-8 declaration, CDATA and comments dropped, decoded entities that can produce invalid XML; validation only parses.
content:
The site's XML formatter re-indents XML, Minify squeezes the structure into a compact form, and Validate only says whether the input parses. All three call DOMParser first, then act separately. This article draws on every case run for it to show what each changes, and why CDATA, namespaces and entities tend to go wrong here.

Formatting: a fixed declaration and two-space indentation

After a successful format the first line is always <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>, immediately followed by the root start tag, with no line break between them. The input's declaration is replaced: given encoding="GBK" and standalone="yes", only the UTF-8 declaration remains. Output is trimmed, so no trailing newline; the status bar reads "Formatting complete" and the counter "71 characters", matching the length of the output string.

Indentation is fixed at two spaces: a four-level sample yields 9 lines, with 8 spaces before the deepest text. An element whose only child is a non-empty text node puts that text on its own line, one level deeper; <a> x </a> becomes three lines, the spaces around x gone, internal spaces and Chinese characters preserved. Empty elements are written <a/>, attribute order unchanged, single quotes turned into double quotes.

Formatting can be run repeatedly, but "byte-identical" has a precondition: when the input contains no entities or character references and no whitespace characters in attribute values that XML parsing would normalize, clicking again on the first output produces an identical second output. With 
 in an attribute value, the first output contains a literal line break, and the second parse normalizes it to a space, so the output changes; input containing & puts a bare & in the first output, and the second parse fails outright. Element names are untouched, and attribute values are kept as DOM values — whitespace normalization and entity decoding during parsing change the literal spelling; text is trimmed only at both ends, and the remaining changes are the declaration, whitespace and attribute quotes; nodes in the next section that are neither elements nor text are skipped wholesale.

Where CDATA, comments and processing instructions go

Formatting and minification handle element and text nodes only. CDATA is its own DOM node type, with no branch in either function, so the section is skipped: <a><![CDATA[x<y>]]></a> formats to only two lines: the first holds the declaration and <a>, the second holds </a>, counted as 46 characters; minified it is <a></a> at 7 characters, with x<y> nowhere in the output.

<a><![CDATA[x<y>]]></a>

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?><a>
</a>

Comments and processing instructions are dropped the same way. <a><!-- note --><b>1</b></a> formats to just the <b> subtree, and a <?xml-stylesheet ...?> before the root never appears. No serializer such as XMLSerializer is used; strings are concatenated by node type, so skipped nodes survive in no form.

Mixed content becomes a block layout: <p>a<b>c</b>d</p> outputs one line each for p, text a, child b and text d, so the inline relationships between a and b, and between b and d, are gone. Read back as text, the output adds extra line breaks and indentation whitespace between a, b and d; XHTML or DocBook paragraphs that depend on inline whitespace do not survive this.

Entity decoding: the output may no longer be valid XML

DOMParser replaces entity references with characters while parsing: & < > become & < >, and AB becomes AB. Formatting splices those characters into the output unchanged, escaping nothing, so <a>& < ></a> yields a bare & and <. Parsing that again gives a parsererror: error on line 2 at column 4: Unexpected token inside entity.

<a>& < ></a>

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?><a>
  & < >
</a>

Attribute values take the same path. Minifying <a b="&"/> gives <a b="&"></a> at 13 characters, and reparsing fails too. Character entities that need no escaping, such as those for letters and digits, are unaffected: AB outputs AB; numeric entities such as & and < still decode to a bare & and <, and a " in an attribute value decodes to a double quote that cuts the attribute value short, so the output can be invalid too; whitespace character references such as 
 become literal line breaks, which affects single-line output and repeated processing, while Chinese characters and internal spaces are preserved as-is. The fault is the missing re-escape: concatenation, unlike a serializer, does not turn &, < and > in character data back into entity references.

So do not save formatting output back as valid XML. After decoding, output with a bare & or < only looks reformatted; it no longer parses. The tool does not check the output either: if the input parses, it says "Formatting complete".

Minification: one line, no declaration, empty elements rewritten

Minification recurses from documentElement, writes <tag attrs>, trims and appends text, then joins it into one line (newlines inside text stay). It writes no declaration, whitespace between tags disappears, and a multi-line sample becomes the 29-character <root><a>1</a><b>2</b></root>; empty <a/> becomes <a></a> at 7 characters.

<root><a>1</a><b>2</b></root>

Minification also drops CDATA, comments and processing instructions, trimming text at both ends but keeping internal spaces. <a> x <b> y </b> z </a> becomes <a>x<b>y</b>z</a> at 17 characters: inter-element whitespace is deleted and x, y, z sit against the tags. Attribute order and values stay, as do bare characters from decoding.

Minifying the same input repeatedly usually gives the same result, but this has a precondition too: only when the input contains no entities or character references, no whitespace characters in attribute values that would be normalized, and the first output still parses does the second minification match the first; line breaks inside a text node stay in the output, so the result is not strictly one line; minified output can also contain a bare & or < (minifying & gives &, for example), and minifying that output again fails to parse and keeps the previous output. Like formatting, it only shortens structure, with no guarantee that the output is still valid XML or that the meaning is unchanged.

The Validate button and namespaces

Validate parses once: on success the status bar reads "XML is valid"; on failure, "Invalid XML: " plus the parsererror text, cut to 100 characters; when the input is whitespace only, "Please enter XML". Only Validate blocks empty input: formatting and minification treat blank input as a parse failure, likewise open with "Invalid XML: ", and keep the previous output. Validation writes nothing to the output box and only updates the status bar.

The tool does no namespace handling itself, but string-level information survives. For <ns:Envelope xmlns:ns="urn:example"> the tagName is still ns:Envelope and xmlns:ns is written as an ordinary attribute; under a default namespace like <a xmlns="urn:x"> children keep no prefix and remain <b>. Bindings are not recomputed; tagName and attributes are merely concatenated.

Limits and constraints

Start with what the buttons promise. Formatting replaces and fixes the declaration and rearranges whitespace and attribute quotes; minification compresses structure. Neither keeps CDATA, comments or processing instructions, re-escapes text, or checks the output's validity. "Formatting complete" and "Minification complete" only mean parsing and concatenation finished, not that the document's meaning survived.

What cannot be configured matters too: indentation is fixed at two spaces, the declaration at UTF-8, blank lines between elements cannot be kept, quotes are always double; no switch keeps or drops CDATA or comments. Mixed content, scripts in CDATA and older documents that rely on whitespace should not be round-tripped.

  • CDATA, comments and processing instructions are not kept, and skipping them produces no warning;
  • text is not re-escaped, so output with a bare & or < may not be valid XML;
  • there are no settings for indent width, declaration content or blank lines between elements;
  • the output is not checked for validity, nor is the meaning before and after compared.

Local processing and the request boundary: this run recorded 12 requests, all same-origin static assets, 0 cross-origin and 0 POST; input exists only in the text box and is lost on refresh or close. The copy button reads the output box and triggers no extra request.

Side by side, the differences come down to a few items:

ItemFormatMinify
XML declarationFixed to UTF-8, replaces the input declarationNot written
Indentation and line breaksTwo spaces, the root element on the declaration's line, one line per level below itWhitespace between tags removed, usually one line
Empty elementsWritten self-closing as <a/>Expanded to <a></a>
TextTrimmed, on its own lineTrimmed, tight against the tags
CDATA, comments, processing instructionsNot writtenNot written
EntitiesWritten as-is after decodingWritten as-is after decoding
AttributesOrder and values kept, double quotesOrder and values kept, double quotes
Trailing newlineNoneNone

If the goal is converting structure rather than layout, the site's JSON/XML/YAML converter handles field mapping and type loss, not whitespace; an HTML fragment can go through the HTML formatter, but its error tolerance differs from an XML parser's, so do not treat the same input in both tools as equivalent.

Whether to use it depends on the next step: formatting suffices for reading or diffing; before handing output to a strict XML parser, XSLT or a SOAP service, confirm there is no bare & or <, and if needed use the original input or an escaping serializer. If the document depends on CDATA, comments or mixed content, do not run these buttons at all; the tool page offers no way to turn those behaviours off.

faqs.q: Why do CDATA and comments disappear after formatting?
faqs.a: Formatting's pretty() emits only element and text nodes, so when it meets CDATA, a comment or a processing instruction it returns immediately and those nodes vanish with their content. Minification's walk() likewise handles only elements and text. When you need to keep this content, do not use these two buttons; the page has no option to preserve or disable it.

faqs.q: Why are the XML declaration and the root tag on the same line?
faqs.a: format() pushes the fixed declaration into the lines array first, then calls pretty() on documentElement from depth 0; pretty() appends the root tag without a leading newline, and the final join("") glues the two together, so the first line is declaration plus root tag. Indentation applies only below the root element, and the page offers no switch to change this layout.

faqs.q: Does XML with namespaces still work after formatting?
faqs.a: Prefixes and xmlns declarations survive as strings: ns:Envelope stays ns:Envelope, xmlns:ns is written out as an ordinary attribute, and children in a default namespace still carry no prefix. The tool does not recompute namespace bindings, but the single parse behind the Validate button is namespace-aware: an unbound prefix raises a parsererror (for example, <ns:a>1</ns:a> reports Element ns:a prefix is unbound); it does not check the output, the schema or business constraints. If the input relies on CDATA, comments or entities, still check the output against the limits described in this article.

faqs.q: Does "XML is valid" mean the output is ready to use?
faqs.a: No. Validation calls DOMParser once and looks for a parsererror; it does not inspect the formatted or minified output, and it does not check the schema or business constraints. A document with escaped entities may parse as valid, yet the formatted output contains a bare &, so the output has to be parsed again to confirm; if the input has an unbound prefix, validation reports an error, but it does not verify that the output is still well-formed.

focus: The XML formatter always emits a UTF-8 declaration and two-space indentation and keeps only element and text nodes; CDATA, comments and processing instructions are dropped. Decoded entities are pasted back as-is, so output containing a bare & or < may no longer be valid XML. Minification removes the declaration, expands every empty element into an open/close pair and squeezes everything onto one line. Validation only asks whether the input parses: it does not check the output, nor whether namespace bindings still hold.
